defects.description: ALB to Fargate edge uses plain HTTP, which contradicts the explicit 'TLS everywhere' requirement (R4); ALB target groups support HTTPS to targets and the design should use it.

Single NAT Gateway serves private tasks in both AZs; if its AZ fails, tasks in the other AZ lose egress (e.g. to Secrets Manager), undermining the two-AZ deployment. Use one NAT gateway per AZ or VPC endpoints.
Route 53 rationale says it resolves the hostname 'over HTTPS'; DNS resolution is not HTTPS.
Audit log tamper-evidence (I1) relies on versioning and log file validation only; S3 Object Lock or a separate log archive account would be stronger for a bank.
No alarms on WAF blocks or failed sign-ins, no WAF logging, and CloudWatch Logs encryption with the CMK is not stated although 'all data' must use bank-controlled keys.
Shield Standard only covers L3/L4; L7 DDoS relies on WAF rate-based rules, which are not mentioned explicitly.

reviews.summary: Sound, well-scoped regulated portal design (WAF+ALB+Cognito MFA, private Fargate, CMK-encrypted Aurora, validated CloudTrail), but it breaks TLS-everywhere on the ALB-to-task hop and has a single-AZ NAT.

defects.description: Single NAT Gateway serves private tasks in both AZs despite the stated Multi-AZ goal (R11); loss of its AZ removes egress for the other AZ.
Shield rationale says the DDoS requirement is met 'at the edge', but there is no CloudFront; the ALB is a regional resource and Shield Standard covers only L3/L4.
Route 53 -> ALB edge labelled HTTPS invoke; DNS only resolves the name, clients connect to the ALB. The customer actor is also missing from the diagram.
KMS key is said to encrypt secrets but no Secrets Manager-KMS link is drawn; CloudWatch Logs CMK encryption not stated.
Audit tamper-evidence (log file validation, Object Lock) is not mentioned for the CloudTrail trail.

reviews.summary: Complete, security-hardened design with HTTPS end to end, Cognito MFA on the ALB, CMK encryption, CloudTrail with lifecycle archive and operational alarms; main weakness is a single NAT gateway.

defects.description: WAF is attached to the API Gateway stage only; the main public entry point is CloudFront, and the API stage remains directly reachable, bypassing edge caching unless restricted.
DynamoDB Streams -> Lambda -> SQS -> Lambda for a welcome email is more moving parts than needed for an infrequent event; a stream-triggered sender with on-failure destination would suffice.

Customer managed KMS key on S3 behind CloudFront and on SQS queues targeted by S3 notifications requires key policies granting CloudFront and S3 kms permissions; not called out, and a CMK adds cost without a stated need.
No Route 53/custom domain and no explicit mention of CloudFront cache policies for the API.

reviews.summary: Correct, robust serverless blog with CloudFront caching, OAC, presigned uploads, prefix-filtered S3->SQS->Lambda thumbnails and DLQs with alarms; slightly over-engineered on the email path.

defects.description: Photo Bucket ObjectCreated events trigger the Thumbnail Function, which writes thumbnails back into the same bucket with no prefix filter or separate bucket, creating a recursive invocation loop.
Photo Bucket is not a CloudFront origin, so photos and thumbnails are not delivered or cached at the edge for a global audience.
Signup function writes DynamoDB then enqueues SQS as two separate calls (dual write); a failure between them loses the welcome email. The rationale dismissing streams is weak.
KMS node is not used by any resource (all encryption AWS-managed); Cognito sign-in for subscribers is unnecessary friction; no presigned-URL issuance edge; no DLQ-to-CloudWatch alarm edges.
Readers node carries an author presigned-upload configuration; actor modelling is inconsistent.

reviews.summary: Reasonable serverless layout with Route 53, CloudFront and async email, but the thumbnail trigger writes into its own source bucket without a prefix filter and photos bypass the CDN.

defects.description: Fargate service, RDS Proxy and Aurora are each placed in a single AZ subnet in the diagram although the rationale says they span two AZs; RDS Proxy needs subnets in at least two AZs.
Encryption in transit for ElastiCache and TLS from ALB to tasks not stated; cache encryption is AWS-managed only.
Two NAT gateways plus WAF add fixed cost; justified by the AZ-loss requirement but not discussed. VPC endpoints for ECR/Secrets Manager could cut NAT data charges.
Cache edge typed 'read' though sessions are also written.

reviews.summary: Solid Multi-AZ Fargate design with ALB, per-AZ NAT for payments egress, Aurora PostgreSQL behind RDS Proxy using Secrets Manager rotation, and Multi-AZ ElastiCache.

defects.description: RDS Proxy has no Secrets Manager edge although it authenticates to the database with Secrets Manager credentials (or IAM auth); with rotation this link is essential.
Only AZ A tasks are shown reading Secrets Manager; AZ B tasks also need credentials.
I3 promises an audit trail of secret access but no CloudTrail is included; CloudWatch alone does not record Secrets Manager API access.
Clients -> WAF edge models WAF as a network hop; WAF is attached to the ALB. App and data tiers share the same private subnets.
RDS Proxy and Aurora drawn in a single AZ subnet; ElastiCache encryption in transit not stated.

reviews.summary: Correct Multi-AZ Fargate/Aurora/ElastiCache design with a CMK and per-AZ NAT, but with a few missing links (RDS Proxy secrets, CloudTrail for the stated audit requirement).

preference.why: B keeps TLS on every hop including ALB to tasks, adds alarms and audit log lifecycle, while A uses HTTP to tasks against the TLS-everywhere requirement; both share the single-NAT weakness.

A's thumbnail pipeline is prefix-filtered and buffered with SQS and DLQs and serves media via CloudFront, whereas B's thumbnail function writes into its own triggering bucket (recursion risk) and photos bypass the CDN.
Both meet the core needs; A wires RDS Proxy to Secrets Manager and separates data subnets, while B leaves gaps in secret access edges and its stated audit requirement.
